utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Tieger, I was informed that you'd like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there is a -- an oral application for protective measures that needs to be brought to the attention of the Court. This is an application for protective measures for KRAJ 682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Prosecution seeks from the Trial Chamber to permit KRAJ 682 to testify with a pseudonym and with image and voice distortion and in private session for those parts of his testimony which are reasonably likely to reveal his identity. I would note that the Trial Chamber has previously held most recently on 4 July 2005 that the existence of the requisite objectively grounded risk to the security of a witness or the witness's family can be demonstrated through a combination of the following factors, with which I know the Court is familiar: Possibility of antagonising persons who continually reside in the territory, for example, by implicating such persons; the fact that the protective witness or his family lives in that territory or have property in that territory or concrete plans to return; and also a general security situation which is unstable and is particularly unfavourable to witnesses and the families of such witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with respect to more precise information, I would ask that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are in open session again. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally in relation to point 3, we note the January 2005 UNHCR report which has been previously submitted to the Chamber. The Chamber has indeed considered the report in coming to the view that the climate in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is set out in the report, remains unfavourable to persons who are resident there or who have family resident there and who wish, nevertheless, to fully discharge their duty to testify before the Tribunal. Your Honour, the Defence has informed us on -- and I think that was on 13 July, that they do not oppose this application strictly to the extent specified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I take it that Mr. Tieger informed the Chamber well about the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Two things. First of all, I appreciate the rigorous way in which it's been dealt with this morning, with appropriate things being in private session and appropriate things being in open session. And that is the Defence's position. We say no more, Your Honour, except that we -- we don't oppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will give a decision as soon as possible. Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, which is a witness without protective measures, as far as I understand, and would be Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say there is one point that I want to raise. I'm sorry. I know the Trial Chamber likes to have notice, so I'm, afraid, in a rush, and being unable break through security this morning; I just overlooked mentioned that to Ms. Philpott. But it would only take about one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps the usher could already prepare the witness to be stand-by. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just really to notify Your Honours, rather than to enter into elaborate submissions this morning, that having looked at the transcript at page 16545, Your Honours gave instructions -- that's at 9 -- at line 11 in relation to the witness -- he was not a protected witness, was -- no, Mr. Davidovic, Your Honour. The Defence is therefore instructed to inform the Chamber by the 21st of July - that's this Thursday - of all information it had available that could shed light on the allegations of misbehaviour and so on. Your Honour, the position is that there is the question of privilege, Your Honour, and may we respectfully suggest that that instruction, if implemented or if followed, would intrude upon privilege and the Defence are entitled and certainly that is our position at the moment, Your Honour, to assert privilege in relation to such information. Accordingly, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, we are not in a position to comply with that instruction as it's expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You certainly noticed that we gave an opportunity to do that in an ex parte way. We'll consider how to deal with this matter at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- perhaps we haven't solved the problem at all, Your Honour. It's ex parte --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise I -- but then we'd like to hear brief submissions on how you see the relation between privilege, counsel-client privilege, and how you think that the Chamber could serve the interests of the witness in a proper way because if finally the Chamber would have to accept that on the basis of privileged material you can put everything to a witness, then, of course, we might have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say straight away, just a simple practical matter: I saw Mr. Hannis briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In that usual meeting Place, the canteen, Your Honour, a few minutes ago. I mentioned to him that I was going to mention this point in case he wanted to come. But, Your Honour, I indicated that I was only at this point intending to mention this point. So if Your Honour is -- is now seeking further submissions, it seems that it would only be right to arrange some time when Mr. Hannis, who's been dealing with this matter for the Prosecution, has the opportunity of being here, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Chamber would like to hear more, especially on the ways the Defence considers the Chamber is able to keep control over the proceedings. If you put to a witness that he's a criminal, if you put to the witness that he personally has stolen matters from others, and if this seems to be contradicted by those who were the victims, the alleged victims, of such behaviour, it would need some further thought on how to deal with this matter because simply saying, This is privileged information, therefore we can't even give a glimpse on what our factual basis existed, and then leave it entirely to the parties to treat a witness in -- well, let me say it, in a firm way, even where later on some information comes to the surface which casts, at least, doubt on whether there were sufficient grounds to treat the witness that way, that might not be a good solution. But I need to give it further thought, and the parties are invited to also further consider how the parties think the Chamber could meet its duties in this respect under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one very important thing that I should say straight away without elaborating in submissions, and that's -- that's this: In relation to how the Trial Chamber can, in a nutshell, protect witnesses, strike the right balance. One very important consideration, Your Honour, is that subject to matters which are under current consideration in this particular Trial Chamber, parties are represented by counsel. I and my co-counsel, Ms. Loukas -- Ms. Loukas is a member of the bar of New South Wales; I'm a member of the bar of England and Wales. Not surprisingly, having a common background, our codes of conduct in this respect are very similar. Our codes of conduct make specific provision in relation to this matter, and that is itself -- the standing and background and integrity and code of conduct binding counsel are themselves a very important protection for the proceedings and for the Trial Chamber. It has been expressly stated by Mr. Hannis that he doesn't allege - and it would be astonishing if he did allege, in fact - any lack of good faith on counsel's part in dealing with this matter -- Your Honour, I, as lead counsel - and I have taken the opportunity over the weekend; I think I said I would, but even if I didn't, I have done - to consider the matter with my co-counsel. We have looked at the material. Your Honour, it's all a matter of judgement in the end, but I am entirely satisfied that there was no question of any breach of counsel's obligations in relation to -- to this matter. And so there may be, then, matters raised by the Prosecution as to where one goes from there in the light of material that they might have unearthed or how one retrospectively looks at it. I touched on some of that the other day. But, Your Honour, the basic and important position is that counsel considers material before putting questions in cross-examination. Counsel knows his or her obligations, and, Your Honour, as far as I am concerned in this case, counsel has met those obligations. Where the matter goes from there, then, is -- I'd suggest, if there is to be further elaboration, further submission, it would be fair that Mr. Hannis, who's dealing with the matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- should then participate. But that is our position at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll further consider the matter, and also if this will be the final view. It might be that the Chamber in controlling the examination of witnesses will be less liberal in allowing, well, let's say, firm allegations put to a witness and would invite the parties to limit itself to factual matters rather than to strong qualifications of the possible behaviour of witnesses. But we'll consider the matter, as I said before; it needs more thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is a very large question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and thought needs time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The one that Your Honour has just raised is a very large question, and it is very dangerous territory, with the utmost respect, for a Trial Chamber in relation to counsel defending a man on the gravity of charges which Mr. Krajisnik faces. And I sincerely submit and hope, Your Honour, that such a -- a important and potentially dangerous issue should be given the most careful and thorough examination before any rulings are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We certainly will do that. At the same time, Mr. Stewart, you'll be aware that it's also a very dangerous matter to let a witness leave this courtroom after they have publicly been alleged to be criminals, go home with that, and especially if it's then said that there were good reasons to put that to him. We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, it isn't a dangerous matter in the hands of responsible counsel, and that is precisely my point, Your Honour. It is not. The danger is obviated by the proceedings being conducted by responsible counsel bound by that code of conduct. That is the whole point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that counsel is behaving -- and I think that the Chamber never suggested that. But the Chamber wants to find out what, then, caused -- well, first of all, the Chamber would like to have facts available. That's most important before saying anything else, and that's what the Chamber asked for. We'll consider the matter. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's all I was going to suggest, Your Honour. I mean, the exchange between the Chamber and Mr. Stewart obviously provokes some thoughts of my own, and I chose not to intervene because I -- the suggestion that we wait for Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to be here and for more thoughtful submissions to be offered is a wise one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Neskovic can be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. But the interpreters can't hear the speaker, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand because you're too far away from the microphone and the microphones are not switched on, anyhow. Mr. Neskovic, before you give evidence, I first for the transcript say that I heard you say "da, da," which means "yes, yes." So you can understand me. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neskovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Tieger, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'd like to begin by providing the Chamber with some general idea of your educational and political background. We can probably deal with that most efficiently if I simply recite to you what I understand to be some of the salient points and you indicate at the end whether or not I have described that history accurately and, if necessary, provide any additional details that seem particularly significant. Now, I understand that you completed high school in Ilidza in 1975 and that you entered the Faculty of Political Sciences in Sarajevo in 1976 and completed your degree in 1978; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your basic occupation since 1979 has been in the area of researching public opinion in television; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to your involvement in politics, is it correct that you were -- although you were -- that you were not a participant in the very earliest stages of the establishment of the SDS party in Bosnia and Herzegovina which you understood to have been formed under the direct influence of the SDS Croatia, which was then under the authority of Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At some point after the 10th of August, I became active within that party, in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in August of 1990, at that time were you informed that a branch of the SDS was to be established in Pale by the initiate board of the SDS and you gave a speech at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on that same day, did Radovan Karadzic ask you if you wanted to become a member of the SDS and explain to you that he envisioned your role would be to conduct research and analysis of public opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I signed the membership card for the SDS as early as the 12th of July, 1990, but until August I was not really an active member. But after my speech at Pale on the 10th of August, Radovan did ask me whether I would like to take on analytical tasks within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after that point, working in that capacity, did you begin attending meetings of the Main Board, at the invitation of Dr. Karadzic, meetings which were held in the Hotel Serbia in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On July 31st, 1991, were you elected as the deputy chairman or deputy president of the Executive Committee of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly was on the 12th of June, and then there was the board, which was set up, and the president was Rajko Dukic, and I was elected deputy president of the Executive Committee. I can't remember the exact date when that happened; possibly on the 31st of July, in fact. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And as a minor matter, our transcript says that the Assembly was on the 12th of June. Was that -- did you mean the 12th of June, or was that the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I meant July. On the 12th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that time, were -- in July of 1991, were you also selected as a member of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you one of the people who was nominated by the general electorate, or were you nominated by an individual?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the entire body that made nominations, but you could make proposals in a twofold way: You were either proposed by some municipal organisations, some grass roots organisation as a member of this main board, or you could have been proposed by the president of the party. I was on the list of names drawn up by the president of the party, and then that list would be voted on, as well. In other words, he could not make a decision single-handedly for us to be appointed to the Main Board; he could just make proposals, and then the Assembly would vote on those proposals, and they would make a selection out of a number of candidates. So Mr. Karadzic was a proponent for myself and a number of other people, and then our names were put to the vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was the provision that permitted the president of the party to nominate persons for the Main Board one that had existed at the time of the initial establishment of the Main Board in 1990, or was it a new provision that emerged in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a new provision from 1991, and that statute was approved on the occasion of that Assembly, and up until 1990 the party had no actual programme, statute, or anything like that, and no systemic acts. So it is a statute that was actually approved on that very day, and it was a new provision from 1991, on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I ask you what the purpose of that provision was. Was it to provide the president of the party with greater control over who was on the Main Board or for some other purpose?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The way I understood it, it was a different reason. There was a problem of insuring democracy, of making sure that people appointed to the Main Board would be democratically elected. And so, of course, to some extent it limited the competencies of the head of the party. On the other hand, we wanted to come up with a compromise between the democratic principle at the grassroots level and also make it possible for the head of the party to have certain competencies in order to avoid a situation whereby he would have absolute power. He was entitled to make proposals for up to one-third of members of the Main Board, and I think according to the statute at the time the Main Board had about 40 people, and so the influence on the part of the president of the party could be up to one- third and the remaining two-thirds would be elected independently of his will on the basis of the electoral mechanicians within the party. And if I may, I would like to add another point in this respect. There were people who were active within the party or were somehow significant, and they had no constituency, as it were. They were not leaders in the field. They could have been experts, lecturers, professors or something like that, and they could not have been proposed. Their names could not have been put forward by a constituency because they didn't have one, and so that was another reason why the President was entitled to propose those names because they might have been dutiful to the party but only up to one-third of the overall membership of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before that provision was enacted as the Assembly, were nominees to the Main Board made by the municipalities and the electorate or made by the president?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Board, as it was initially set up, I think was decided upon at the constitutional Assembly in July 1990 at the meeting at Skenderija. But there were no real rules, so those people who were the most active as the party was being set up were swept into the Main Board. And the party was actually created by a merger of a number of other small parties on the 12th of July, 1990, so they tried to make them happy, as well, by taking their members or leaders. So I think the first Main Board, the original one, I think, was rather big. Quite a few people were there. So those people were swept into power, as it were, because they happened to be there at the time. So it wasn't based on any rules or documents because back in 1990 the party did not have any statute, any rules of procedure or anything. They did not have a programme. And it had not even been officially registered at the time. So it was a rather chaotic situation at the -- at the founding Assembly back in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to some additional positions you held. In 1992, did you serve as president of the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In July of 1992 -- well, in that connection actually, let me take this opportunity to ask that you be provided with a binder that contains certain documents. And if that has not already been distributed to the Court, I would ask that that be done now. Mr. Neskovic, as the usher has indicated to you, that document contains -- or that binder contains various documents which are separated by tabs, and I will refer you to tab numbers as I ask you to look at particular documents. In this case, I would direct your attention to the document contained behind tab number 1 and ask you at the same time whether you became a member of the war commission for the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo in July of 1992 and specifically on 21 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Although, it is not even clear to me today, not to this day, what this war commission was all about, what was its purpose and what they were supposed to be doing. Mr. Katic was there; Mr. Skrba Panjevic. It was a body which was presumably set up in July by the president. It was not very active down there, and to this day, to be honest, I don't really know what it was all about because at that period of time, at Grbavica in particular, in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Committee for the municipality had already been set up. So in other words, there were legal municipal bodies in existence. So I really don't know what the purpose of that war commission was, considering that we had legally elected municipal bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note that the document at tab 1 is Exhibit P64.A or at least contained within the body of the documents in P64.A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, the document refers to a republican commissioner who was to hold the position of chairman of that war commission. Do you recall who that person was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may take a moment to concentrate a little bit because there was a great deal of cowice [as interpreted] at that time. Well, there was this notion of the Crisis Staff, and there was the notion of the War Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me a second. To help you to focus this examination, I will be going through the Crisis Staff with you in greater detail in my later questions, so it's not necessary, unless it's absolutely -- unless you think it's absolutely necessary to answer this question, to delve into that now. So -- and I'll certainly give you an opportunity to concentrate on this particular question, but I just ask you for the moment to focus on who the republican commissioner was for Novo Sarajevo in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: There were two types of commissionerships, as it were. I think one commission was appointed by the government, and it was one person, in fact, one commissioner who was acting on behalf of the government. And the other commission was set up, and it included a number of people, including myself, Panjevic and the others. And the person appointed by the government, I think, was Professor -- Dr. Milimir Mucibabic. So there was a kind dual-track approach. It was slightly unclear because there was a commission set up by the President, and in parallel there was this commission set up by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucibabic leave? And if so, who took over for him after that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mucibabic was there only once. There was one huge meeting which had been organised, and there were quite a few problems that cropped up. I think maybe we can come back to those later. I got the impression that he as a person disagreed with the leadership, which appointed him in the first place, and soon afterwards he left the area and went to Belgrade. Thereupon, if I remember correctly, it was either Vladimir Lukic and Dragan Djokanovic; I'm not sure who was the direct successor. Perhaps initially Vlado Lukic, and then afterwards Dragan Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I don't know if it will -- if it helps to clarify your answer at all - and you'll have to tell us whether it does - but I would note at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. page 113 of the interview that you conducted with representatives of the Prosecution you said that Milimir Mucibabic was the official before Dragan Djokanovic, so Djokanovic was after Mucibabic. Does that refresh your recollection at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mucibabic was there before, in fact, and very briefly. But as to whether he was succeeded by Djokanovic and then Lukic or the other way around, I can't remember. But Mucibabic was the commissioner, that's for sure, and he remained in that position for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally completing our brief discussion of the positions you held, if I could ask you to turn to the document contained at tab 2 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if that could be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab number 2 will be Prosecution Exhibit P895.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, the document before you now, Prosecution 895, is a document entitled "Conclusion of assignments per domain of the members of the Executive Board dated 24 February 1993," and it lists a number of specific assignments and a number of individuals who are assigned. Let me ask you first if this accurately reflects your membership of the SDS Executive Board in February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Up to February 1993, there was this re-privatisation of commodities reserves, but I had nothing to do with it whatsoever. I was a member of the party, and since February 1993 I continued in the same job I had in 1991; I was a kind of party activist who travelled around trying to solve organisational or staff issues in various municipalities. I attended a number of municipal meetings all over the place, and so I was a party activist. And Jovo Sarac was a capable lawyer, so with regard to this privatisation of reserves, I really don't think that I myself or Jovo Sarac, basically, had nothing to do with it; no practical link to this, at any rate. And we never dealt with this at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you considered a de facto member of the Executive Board at that time? And if not, how was it that the members of the Executive Board assigned you this task?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a de facto member of the Executive Board. But with regard to practical tasks assigned on the occasion of our meetings, with regard to commodity reserves or re-privatisation, it had never been mentioned to me. I never dealt with it at all. I really don't know how these line duties came about, which had nothing to do with anything in practice. Perhaps I missed something; perhaps I wasn't following things properly. But in what I did, in practice, I had absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with what is contained in this document. And let me tell you, it is rather illogical. Why would the members of the Executive Board deal with the commodities reserve, since it is within the area of competence of the government at that time, all types of resources, including material resources, and that includes commodities reserves, felt within the exclusive area of competence of the government, that is to say, the Minister of Trade and Industry. And so it would be a bit ridiculous for a member of the Executive Committee at a time of war to deal with something and to interfere with something that is within the exclusive and sole area of competence of the government. So it is not really logical, and it has nothing to do with the real situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Ostojic still the Minister of Information at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. At the time, I think he was no longer Information Minister. He himself and Miroslav Toholj kind of succeeded one another. I can't remember, but I think Ostojic was perhaps a minister without portfolio or something like that or -- at any rate, the president of the Executive Committee was Jovo Mijatovic. Ostojic might have had a role because he was Minister of Information the previous government. So he probably had some kind of link with the government. But it doesn't really make sense because all the liaising with the government went through Karadzic and Krajisnik, as top officials. Why would president of a government deal with the Executive Committee members since it is being done by somebody else? So it is less than clear to me, I'm afraid. Perhaps after the meeting of the Executive Board this was written in such a way as to not fully reflect what took place in the course of the discussions at the Executive Board. Ostojic might have been active in some way; I can't be sure. Either he was in the government as a minister without portfolio or he was some kind of liaison official between the government and the Executive Committee, even though that doesn't make sense, either because why would a body of the party and government have to do any liaising? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you know, what was Mr. Ostojic supposed to do about migrations and depopulation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you specify at what period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me focus first on the time he received this assignment, February 24th, 1993. It appears that part of his assignment is migrations and depopulation, and I'm wondering if you can shed light on that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were other bodies in place at the time dealing with migrations. I think that we had some kind of committee or some kind of commission for the refugees, for taking care of the refugees. All I can say is that he had to be given something to do. I think providing for the displaced population, but I think I can stick to my own personal opinion, in the sense that this was indicated as one of his competencies, just so -- in order to give him something to do because he was one of the candidates for the post of the president and he was not elected. Jovo Mijatovic was elected. And to be quite honest, I have no idea what he could have been doing back in 1993 in relation to the displaced persons, staff issues, or migration. I don't know, really, what kind of migration -- I'm not familiar with the details of his job, what did he, in fact, do on a daily basis in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn now to some questions about the party itself, its structure and hierarchy. First of all, is it correct that the main -- the principal bodies of the SDS party would have been the Main Board, the Executive Board, the Municipal Boards, and the local boards, and if there are any other bodies within the party that are significant, please identify those for us.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may make a correction here, according to the statute from 1991, the 12th of July, that is, the top body within the party was the Assembly, then the Main Board. It was the biggest and the most significant body in between the Assembly meetings, and the Executive Committee was an executive body of the Main Board, an executive arm of the Main Board, so it stood for the continuity, in terms of the routine tasks to be carried out by the party in between meetings of the Main Board, and certainly this was a body with considerable competencies within the party. And after the 12th of July, 1992, there had been far-reaching reforms within the structure of the party. Up until 1991, the party wasn't -- rather big, a popular movement, as it were, without a proper party structure, and radical reforms were implemented at that electoral Assembly. And two key principles were decided upon on that occasion, one of them being that the main structure or the -- the basic body would be a local community or a local committee and not a municipal one. So they would start at the very lowest rung of the ladder if they wanted to make their way and have a proper career within the party; that was in order to cut down on the red tape and in order to avoid any one small group getting absolute power. So the basic structure of the -- or the basic part of the party structure was this local committee, so that was the most important body at the local level; whereas, the president had the most power at the global level, so to say. And the second principle, which was decided upon on the 12th of July, 1991, was a clear distinction between the executive powers and the party power, so no single official of the party could be within the executive power structure of the state and the other way around. Only one part of the MPs - I think maybe up to ten - could be MPs and members of the Main Board at the same time. And as to the executive positions and the party positions, there was a clear distinction there. And so, for example, a minister could not have been on the Main Board or the Executive Committee or, for example, a member of the Executive Committee could be deputy police chief. So those were the two main principles. And there was another novelty that had been introduced; that is to say, this local committee. And then there were lots of arguments about the conflict of interest and the principle of democracy and the principle of leadership. Karadzic, as the leader, of course wanted to have as much power as possible, to be the head of the party, and there was some resistance, as well. And so that's how the compromise was reached; that is to say, to have democratically elected members, up to two-thirds, that is to say, of membership, and Karadzic would have been entitled to put forward the names and select up to one-third of this membership. And so that's -- that was the compromise that was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, in your answer you -- you mentioned the SDS Assembly, the Main Board. You emphasised the role of the local boards. You didn't mention the Municipal Boards, but was that the body immediately above the local boards?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And was -- was that a higher -- I mean, you alluded to it in your answer, but I just want to confirm whether or not that was a hierarchical structure, that is, whether or not orders went down from the top, through those bodies that you mentioned, ultimately to the local boards.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are activities in both spheres. At the top of the party, President Karadzic, who pursued his policies, tried to ensure that legal principles were followed in the broad party organs when he took decisions, so he tried to act at the top, but a lot of initiatives were taken at the municipal level. And then at the Main Board, these principles would face each other. There was a principle of democratic centralisation. There was a lot of democracy until a decision was taken, and when a decision was taken, then the usual party hierarchy was implemented. This hierarchy was in place. Once the decision was taken, once a decision had been agreed on, then it was necessary for this decision to be implemented by all the bodies, by the local board, by the Municipal Board. Sometimes there were Regional Boards in place, as well. So I would call this a principle of democratic centralisation. The principles followed were democratic until a decision was taken. But once a decision had been taken, the decision would be implemented; the hierarchy had to be respected. I'd just add that the Main Board could also dismiss municipal bodies if they believed that they were not functioning correctly or failing to implement the party's policies. According to the statute, they had such power and they could call elections to form a new body at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, of course, there were elections in 1990 for positions within the political structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which the three main parties participated. Did the elections of 1990 and the subsequent assumption of positions within the political authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina by members of the SDS have an impact on the -- on who made decisions within the party and which individuals were in control of decisions made with respect to the party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to provide you with a brief explanation, if I may. After the elections - I think that it was in November 1990 - there was a political rule in force, which is quite customary in the world, but in relation to the SDS this rule was a little more radical. The president of the party, Radovan Karadzic, after the elections didn't pay as much attention to the Main and Executive Board; he focussed on members of executive and legislative power who had assumed state positions on behalf of the SDS. He had far more intense contact with Plavsic and Koljevic, as members of the Presidency, and with Krajisnik, as the president of the Assembly, with eight Serbian ministers who are in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He had more contact with functionaries in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina who are acting on behalf of the SDS. So those structures, which on behalf of the SDS started executing state power in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the body that Karadzic had a lot of contact with. But as far as the party itself is concerned, immediately after the elections it was somewhat neglected; it wasn't that important because a member of the Main of Executive Board was no longer important after the elections. The minister was important; the deputy of the MUP minister was important; the president of the Assembly was important, et cetera., so that Karadzic then started focussing on those bodies. And in a certain sense, they all acted together or individually, and after power had been established, they would take all the decisions, agree on policies together with Karadzic. He didn't become part of state power, but he was a figure of authority who had a lot of contact with all the representatives of the power structures. The party leader after the elections would then focus on his representatives within the organs of power, and he would focus less on the party because after the elections, the party was no longer that important. There was a victory at the elections, so they could participate in power. And afterwards it was no longer that important, and it entered a crisis period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Within that group of officials that you mentioned, who, by virtue of their positions or relationship with Dr. Karadzic or for other reasons, were the principal decision-makers or implementers of policy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They seem to be two different things, Your Honour, decision-makers or implementers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Neskovic, if those are two different thing, then please tell us, and if the -- if both of those roles were held in the hands of the same persons, then you can tell us also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I didn't mean they were necessarily two different things. It turns up that they mean two different things as a matter of -- potentially as a matter of language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger asked you who were the principal decision-makers or implementers of policy, and if you say that the decision-makers were not the same as the implementers of policy, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please clarify something. Are you referring to decisions taken at the level of the state or at the level of the party?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I understood you to say, Mr. Neskovic - and, please, do tell us if this is an incorrect understanding - that Dr. Karadzic began to turn and work with persons who held significant positions within the state in order to make decisions and for the -- and perhaps - and you can tell us if that's right too - for enforcement of those decisions within the party.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that his closest associate was the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, and then there was Biljana Plavsic because she held a very important position in the Presidency. She was involved in the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, which is a body that controls the police and the security forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then he also had contact with Koljevic, and then there was the head of the Club of Deputies, Mr. Vojo Maksimovic, and then there was also a prominent deputy, Aleksa Buha. These were individuals who had positions within the state, either legislative positions or executive positions, and they also had good -- a good personal relationship with Karadzic, and that was even the case before the SDS had been established because Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic knew each other and they were on good terms, and this was the case before the SDS was established. There were others whom I do not know. There were people in the MUP, in the Ministry of the Interior. I think there was the deputy Vitomir Zepinic. I think he had some sort of a position in the MUP, that Momcilo Mandic had some sort of a position within the MUP, and there were probably some other municipal functionaries who became representatives of the municipal authorities. So on the whole, these are the people concerned, the people at the highest level, and yes, they had good personal relationships, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Dr. Karadzic's closest associate was Mr. Krajisnik, and you also mentioned his position as president of the Assembly. Was that position significant enough, and was his relationship with Dr. Karadzic close enough so that the two of them together could be said to be the top leaders or supreme authorities of the SDS and the Serb movement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's a fact that they had known each other for a long time before that period; they knew each other very well. This is supported by the fact that from the time the party was established, and right up until the elections, Mr. Krajisnik didn't hold a significant position in the party. He was the president of the Municipal Board in Novi Grad, the president of a local board. And when a list for -- of republican deputies was being compiled, he was the last person on the list. So he barely managed to win at those elections. And up until the elections, within the party structure Krajisnik didn't have a significant position. But immediately after the elections, he suddenly became the president of the Assembly, and he had a high level state position. And I and others believed that he had become the president of the Assembly not thanks to his work within the party but thanks to his personal relationship with Karadzic. And Karadzic became personally involved, ensured that Krajisnik was the president of the Assembly; this was of decisive importance. And there was also a suggestion that Mr. Milan Trbojevic should be the president of the Assembly; he had almost become the president of the Assembly, but then Karadzic changed that decision and prevented Trbojevic from being elected. He personally insisted on Mr. Krajisnik assuming that position. So Krajisnik, who was the president of a Municipal Board, immediately assumed this position after the elections, and the reason for this is his personal relationship with Karadzic and the fact that Karadzic insisted on Krajisnik having that position. So the president of the Municipality in the former system of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the president of the Municipality has an extremely important position because this involves legislative power, constitutional power, executive power. So at the time of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, no important decisions would be taken without the presence of the president of the Assembly. So it was a very important position even before the SDS but also at the time of the SDS. This position is far more important than the position of Prime Minister. I think that this position was more important than the position of a member of the Presidency because there were five or six such members. It was a collective body, and they had to agree on things together, but the position of president of an Assembly is an extremely important position. And later on I would say that Krajisnik and Karadzic were at the highest level of power. I would say that those are the kind of positions they had; that is my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a minor matter - I don't know if this was a translation problem, and I don't know that it requires the witness - but on 29 -- oh, I'm sorry. Excuse me a second. 29, 9 and 10, it states "the president of the Municipality has an important position -- the president of the Municipality in the former system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president of the Municipality has an extremely important position."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I certainly understood the witness to be talking about the president of the Assembly, and I don't know if Mr. Stewart similarly heard that but -- or understood that. I can ask for clarification, or we can have a consensus that that is, in fact, what the witness was talking about. But I see Mr. Stewart doesn't have his earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's not for the first time that the Chamber notes that you're more interested in your conversations at the Defence bench, and when you're even directly addressed by Mr. Tieger you do not even notice that. It's not just on my behalf, but it is on the behalf of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on behalf of the Chamber that I say - and we discussed it several times - that this is certainly not the first time, that you seem to be more interested in your own conversations than to hear what witnesses or counsel for the other party are --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- I didn't realise that. If, of course, I'm being directly addressed by Trial Chamber or counsel for the other party, then naturally I would hope to respond, and that should be brought to my attention. But, Your Honour, I have a number of very urgent and difficult matters to discuss as well as the matters occurring in court, and I have to discuss them with my case manager now, and that is what we were doing. And, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, how I actually use my time in court to deal with such matters is entirely up to me if I don't cause any disruption, Your Honour. And I do not and will not accept directions by the Trial Chamber as to how I should use my time when I'm sitting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't intend any discourtesy, Your Honour, and I am here available to deal with any direct questions or inquiries put to me by the Trial Chamber, my opponents, or anybody. But otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, when I need to discuss these matters with my case manager, that is what I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I would not have referred to any earlier occasion if it had not been a frequent subject of discussion over the last week, which included, sometimes, disruptive character of your private conversations at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if they are disruptive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I am not going to discuss the matter. You were addressed by Mr. Tieger. Could you please respond to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I want you now to respond to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I want to say this. If at any time anything I say is disruptive, then I would welcome that being brought to my attention, Your Honour. But if it is genuinely disruptive, then, of course, I have not the slightest intention -- it would be quite improper for me to conduct myself in court for any way which is disruptive. But it is entirely proper for me to conduct myself privately in conversations with my team, which I need to do. The pressures on this Defence team are such that we have to do about ten things at once in court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I've heard about the matter. Could you please respond to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be grateful then, therefore, to have it pointed out to me what I was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger asked you whether you would agree that there might have been a mistake in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to -- to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was the issue of where the witness -- at least on the transcript it seems that he had spoken about the President of the Municipal Board where he had, as a matter of fact, the President of the Assembly in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can somebody --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Give me the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will. At the lower portions of page 28, there was a discussion by the witness of the selection of the president of the Assembly, and then the witness went on to note that Mr. Krajisnik, who had been a president of a Municipal Board then immediately assumed this position after the elections and the reason for it -- and he explained why that was. And then he began explaining the significance of that position, which I understood to be explaining the significance of the position of president of the Assembly, but the transcript at 29, 6 and 7 says, "So the president of the Municipality in the former system of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the president of the Municipality has an extremely important position because this involves legislative power," et cetera. And then he concludes at 29, 11, obviously talking about "the president of the Assembly." So I just wanted confirmation that those two earlier references to Municipal Board -- to Municipal Board were simply mistranslations and were actually references to president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, so far as mistranslations are concerned, I have to consult my case manager, anyway. I'm not entirely sure whether he was -- whether he was in court in that precise moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he was in conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he hasn't been in court for most of this morning because he's been dealing with the very urgent matter which I needed to discuss with him when he came into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was in the last five minutes, Mr. Stewart. Your case manager was in, but he was engaged in a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For the reasons I've said, Your Honour. Yes, precisely. Well, I'm sorry about that, Your Honour. We'll have to review this later, as often happens when my case manager's not in court. We can't do anything about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- nor can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. And, Mr. Tieger, you can continue at this moment. Let's ask the witness, when you were talking about -- well, perhaps you'd directly ask the witness, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Neskovic, you may have heard a good bit of this exchange and may already know what I'm about to ask you, but when you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say Mr. Krajisnik informs me that in his view it was a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that would be -- it's so logical that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik, for assisting in this way. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, were you aware whether in 1990 and 1991 SDS officials were conducting discussions -- let me ask the question a different way. I'm sorry about that. Did you know whether or not SDS officials were having meetings and discussions with Mr. Milosevic in either 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, up until November 1990, I -- well, I have no information about that, but after the elections, yes. I think that Mr. Karadzic had the most intensive form of contact with him, and he very frequently went to -- to see him. This could be seen quite openly. But Mr. Karadzic also had unlimited possibilities of going there in secret. We are aware of meetings Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that were held openly, and the media would report on them. But as for the secret meetings, we know nothing about them. But there is some information that Mr. Karadzic would provide us with; he'd provide us with selective information after he'd returned from Belgrade, having had discussions with Milosevic there. We thought that the information we were provided with was complete, but with hindsight, we could say that the information that we were provided with by him was selective. In the Main Board, some were against Karadzic going to see Milosevic, and there were some people from the SDS who thought that we shouldn't have any form of contact with Milosevic. They thought that we should pursue our own independent policies in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that if we needed to establish contact with anyone, it should be with Serbs who had emigrated to America and elsewhere. So there were some people who expressed reservations as far as this is concerned, but there was contact between Karadzic and Milosevic from November 1990 right up until perhaps May 1993. They had very frequent contact during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that exclusively Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic, or did someone else participate or engage in those discussions with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether any others had contact with him. Karadzic liked to have informal groups when he had such contact with other individuals. He had good friends of his in Belgrade - Obradovic [phoen], Gojko Djogo [phoen], and so on - and he would often go with them or with his wife or with Koljevic. So Karadzic probably frequently changed the composition of his team, but on the whole he usually spoke to Milosevic on his own. And if a team did go to Belgrade -- because my friend Mr. Micevic was his driver. I asked him how this took place, and he said, The team would reach a building or a waiting room and then Karadzic would go into Mr. Milosevic's office on his own and they would speak there or somewhere else. But on the whole, I think that when they had contact, they were alone or perhaps there were some other people from Belgrade or from the other bodies of power in Serbia; but I don't know the details. But I stand by my claim that they usually spoke to each other alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may direct your attention to an exchange you had with representatives of the OTP in April of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm directing everyone's attention to page 74 of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At that time, you were asked about leaders you had named, including Mr. Milosevic, and you were asked to describe any meetings -- any meetings that -- no, I'm sorry. It won't be contained in there. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can do a couple of things, but it might be best if I just read to you in English so it will be translated the portion of the interview, and then you can respond. As I indicated, you were asked to describe meetings that you had with Mr. Milosevic or that leaders of the Bosnian Serbs had. In your answer, you provided some of the information that you did earlier, but more specifically you said, "But the cooperation outside the party, it was very intensive. They met very often, had contacts and meetings; it was obvious." Then the question was asked: "Who met, and who had these contacts and meetings?" And your answer was, "In most cases, Karadzic and Krajisnik had those contacts because if we asked where they were, we were answered that they went to Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Krajisnik also had contact, but I think that he established such contact with Milosevic later on, after Radovan had established contact with him, and I think that perhaps in 1992, 1993, or 1994 he established contact with him. That's when he had meetings with him. But I can confirm that Krajisnik certainly did see Milosevic but not as frequently as Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note the time. I -- I imagine we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. But if you'd just allow me to finish my annotation on the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, might we have a very slightly longer break than usual because, as a matter of fact, the matters which were arisen this morning do require me to -- to speak to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second for my note, annotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I can concentrate on your question for a longer break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd like to have a slightly longer break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I was really wondering if we can have about ten minutes longer than usual. Your Honour, the matter I was discussing, I don't wish to keep it secret, was in the course of this morning since we arrived Mr. Karganovic has translated that letter for me, which is in Serbian. So I hope, Your Honour, it will be recognised that -- that such -- such conversations in court are, in fact, an essential part of the process of defending Mr. Krajisnik. So, Your Honour, my request, Your Honour, is just to have that slightly longer break so that -- that I can be --

utterances.text: We'll have a break until ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Tieger proceeds with this witness, I just wanted to mention a contextual document and distribute that and obtain an exhibit number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's a document that Mr. Harmon foreshadowed last Thursday, and he distributed a copy to the Defence. It's a contextual document for the witness Ewan Brown, also for Witness KRAJ 30, KRAJ 165, KRAJ 666, and the witness Kuralic, and if we could hand that up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Prosecution Exhibit P896.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Tieger, you can proceed. If distribution can take place, at least a copy for the registrar is most important. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I don't want to spend a great deal of time with the next subject, but I do want to ask you a few questions about the various -- about at least some of the various ways in which the party leadership communicated orders or decisions to the lower levels. And in that connection, if I could turn your attention next to tab 5 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if I could have that marked next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P897.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, tab 5, now P897, reflects the minutes of a meeting of the SDS Assembly in Prijedor held on 3 July 1991, a meeting that was attended by you, as it indicates at the top, a member of the Main Board of the SDS. Let me ask you first, as a general matter, if one of the ways that the leadership communicated its decisions to the various levels below was by sending emissaries, such as yourself, to directly deal with the bodies at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the ways of doing it, though it was regulated; in other words, not just anyone could go and do as they pleased, but the Main Board would entrust one of the members, one from their own ranks or perhaps even an MP who was on the Main Board or, in most cases, a member of the Executive Committee, so that person would be entrusted to go to that specific place and solve the problem that arose there. It was not some kind of relaying of orders. It was simply sending an emissary from higher up within the party to lower-ranking bodies to deal with the practical situation or a problem or carry out a practical task, and thereupon that emissary was supposed to report back and, you know, tell what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to dealing with practical situations or problems or assisting in carrying out practical tasks, what was -- were you engaged in, and was that a general effort to ensure that Municipal Boards were capable of and did implement decisions that had been made earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I was mostly involved in harmonising the work of the Municipal Committee within itself and to do away with any fractions, and since there were quite a few problems there, we were looking to organise some kind of an election and solve that in a democratic fashion. And during that particular period of time, I think I was in charge of organising elections in the area of the municipality of Prijedor, for the Serbian Democratic Party, and for the delegates to be elected for the upcoming electoral Assembly of the SDS at the republican level. That's on the basis of what I can see here. My recollection is that that was my job at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say you were trying to make sure that the whole system was harmonised and functioning as well as it could?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In a way, I took my job at face value, as it were, and my responsibilities, as well, without thinking of any alternatives. If it said in the statute that the elections for the Municipal Board were to take place in a certain fashion, I would stick to those instructions. In other words, we have -- we had to elect the delegates for the local boards and then the Municipal Board, and then they would send off delegates to the republican electoral Assembly, and I did it devotedly and in an honest way. And I always stuck to the rules rigorously, and I spared no effort in that respect, but I never went beyond that particular remit. In other words, I did what I was told to do in a way that it was prescribed, and normally I obtained results because I tended to be both tolerant and persevering in my efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn next to tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would ask that that be marked next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P898.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you been able to find that, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, P898 is a telephone conversation held on 10 September 1991 involving yourself, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Miskovic, and Mr. Srdic, both of whom are from Prijedor. I'll give you a moment to look at that. Let me direct your attention in particular to two portions of that conversation: Immediately after the initial salutations where you're saying hello to Dr. Karadzic and indicate to him that Srdjo - I presume Mr. Srdic - is there, as well, you say, "We'll probably have to take that direction to assign those 15 people, you know." Dr. Karadzic indicates, "Yes." And then you say, "And then the task of the 15 people should be to go to the field and check all the local boards." Is this discussion and your presence in Prijedor at that time a further reflection of the efforts you spoke about earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do actually remember this. There was quite a conflict between the then-president of the Municipal Committee of SDS, Dr. Srdjo Srdic, and another group or a fraction headed by Miskovic, I believe. And I came to see Srdjo Srdic at his flat, and in that flat we had a conversation and I asked him to back off, that if he thought he had a problem and could not continue to lead the Municipal Committee any more and to withdraw because he was elderly and frail. But he was fiercely opposed to that. And then there were phone calls. I called Karadzic, and Srdic called Karadzic, and Karadzic called Miskovic, and so between Neskovic, Srdic and Miskovic and Karadzic there were these conversations going on all the time in all directions. And I don't think we actually managed to achieve anything that very evening after this phone conversation except to appoint 15 people to go and check the situation out in the field. And then we decided that there would be a meeting of the municipal organisation in Prijedor the next day, and there were quite heated and unpleasant discussions on that occasion, as well, and in the end Srdjo Srdic basically withdrew, and he was replaced by Mr. Miskovic. And I think it took a long time. I think I was there two days: One day at Srdic's flat, when all these phone conversations were going on; and the second day at the meeting, where the situation was being solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I ask you to turn next to tab 8. Sorry, we're moving through the binder in that fashion, but it's sometimes necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If that can be marked next in order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 8, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- tab 8. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you allow me just to go back for one second to tab 29, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Neskovic, to look at, what is in the English, the third page. Let me just try to find it in the ... At a certain moment, you say -- I think it's on the second page, the -- let me see -- twelfth box, where Radovan Karadzic says, "Yes. Yes." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean on page 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on page 2. Yes, there's two times when he says "yes, yes," I think, but approximately in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read the next few lines; that means what you say in response to that "because they do not recognise any authority here, especially if you mentioned Sarajevo," then Mr. Karadzic says, after a few unpleasant words, "Let them make their own party; let them resign. Whoever refuses to obey Sarajevo should resign. Write papers for them tomorrow and say, This is a party which has its top and its bottom, and nobody will fuck about under our name." Then you say, "I won't give it to them. I didn't give it to them the last time, either. I'll call Vukic tomorrow to help me with them." And then, "And please tell them this. Please, whoever won't adhere to the policies of the party and implements the policies of the party but adheres to their own private policies." "Yes." And then: "Let them sign here, let them leave that place in the municipality." This very much reflects an atmosphere in which obedience was required from the party at the municipality level. Is that a correct impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Obedience was required, even though Mr. Karadzic seems to have expressed it in his own special way, which tended to complicate matters further and increase the tension to a certain extent. I tried to work in another way and go for a compromise and indicate to people that we had the statute of the party and everybody was supposed to stick to it; whereas, Karadzic based everything on his own personal authority, and he was in conflict with Mr. Milakovic in the past, so whenever Milakovic's name was mentioned he would have an emotional reaction. So in terms of discipline, he was betting on his own personal identity, saying, You have to listen and to be obedient; who doesn't like it has to go. But I thought that this was not the best way for achieving unity but that you should spend time out in the field and talk to people at the grassroots level and listen to people's opinion and try and reconcile the two groups' views. And otherwise my suggestion was for everybody to resign and the elections to be organised so that altogether new people would come along. So I did differ from Mr. Karadzic in terms of how these things should be done out in the field, even though I was a lower-ranking official, and as such I was supposed to obey his orders. But I did decide that I had to have some leeway as to how to do what I was told to do. So we had a different approach to the same problem, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, a few lines further down, you ask him what to do, so you seek his guidance, isn't it? "Tell me, what should we do tomorrow?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They had convened a huge meeting for the following day between two rather extreme groups. One was led by Milakovic, and the other was led by Srdjo Srdic, and therefore I asked him for some kind of guidance as to how to go about it all and how to overcome the problem the next day. And I wanted to know what his attitude was as the head of the party because he could have entitled me to organising fresh elections and -- so I wanted to know what his attitude was, whether he was in favour of sending everybody home and organising the new elections or sticking with the existing two fractions. And he was rather vague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. I'm not interested in all the details of what, but I just noticed that you seek his guidance. The whole atmosphere of this conversation is such that even where you said that you did not -- that you differed from Mr. Karadzic in terms of how these things should be done, that at the same time it was not easy to resist Mr. Karadzic. That's at least the atmosphere that comes from this telephone conversation, that Mr. Karadzic seems to be quite strong in saying how he wants things to be done. Is that a correct understanding, that resisting the wishes or the imperatives of Mr. Karadzic was not an easy thing do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very difficult, and a great deal of diplomatic skill was called for, in terms of either refusing to do something or doing something in a slightly different way and not exactly the way he wanted you to do. He was an undisputed authority, so it wasn't easy; it was rather difficult to contradict him openly and publicly and say, You know what? I refuse to listen to you any more, or, I don't want to continue to talk to you, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be true for all party levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please just clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that on the republican level of the SDS but also the municipal and the local level, wherever there were clear feelings or clear instructions, that it was difficult to resist him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the local level it was very difficult to resist him because there were no high-level political figures that -- no strong personalities, with the exception of a number of individuals whom I could mention. But at the republican level, in the Main Board it was a little different because Karadzic presided over the Main Board, but there were 45 of us there, after all, and the people there were slightly more prominent and capable, and at the Main Board there was resistance. Different opinions were expressed. So it was not that easy to implement the policies -- to get the policies through at the Main Board. At the Main Board, Radovan mostly tried to persuade everyone, and he went to great lengths to do so. Within the Main Board, it was a lot easier to put up resistance, a lot easier than it was at the local level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even in one of your earlier answers you said, "It was very difficult, and a great deal of diplomatic skill was called for in terms of either refusing to do something or to do something or doing something in a slightly different way."
