Was that limited to public debate? Because you say it was very -- "rather difficult to contradict him openly and publicly." That sounds a bit as if it was not that easy, even when you were in direct contact with him, such as at the republican level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the republican level, when the Main Board was in session, various discussions would be held. There was nothing that you would have to do. You would just have to discuss matters, and you could express different opinions. But if you had a particular task assigned to you by Karadzic or the executive or Main Board, if your task was to go into the field and do something in particular there, then it was very difficult to put up resistance if you had a particular task. In order to avoid any misunderstandings, I wanted to know exactly what I had to do, what sort of authority I had, where I had to do it, and when, so that I could be held responsible for what I did, so that I could do what I had to do in a responsible manner. He did not treat me in a rough way. I had a certain amount of freedom to carry out tasks in an independent way. I didn't have the same problems that Srdjo and others had. I don't know whether it was because he had allowed me to act in this manner or whether I had managed to obtain such privileges. But in any event, if someone wanted to resist him, it was necessary to have a lot of courage, and this also meant losing one's position in the Main Board. I'll provide you with the example of Milakovic, who publicly opposed him, resisted him, and he was expelled from the Main Board. And Sladimir Srebrov also resisted him in public before that, and he was also expelled from the Main Board. So you are quite right: It was very difficult to directly oppose him, and usually one would suffer the consequences, and you would be driven away. You would be expelled from that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I had directed your attention to tab 8, a document that was marked as P899. That's a conversation held on 26 September 1991 between Dr. Karadzic and Miroslav Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's indicated in the text, Your Honour, Stancic. I had that checked. It is Stanic, according to the reviewer. And I thought we had prepared a corrected version. If so, it obviously did not make it into the binders, and we'll see it that does. In any event, we'll be talking briefly with the witness about that, and he can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, as the transcript of this conversation indicates at the beginning, that this is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and the gentleman who's the president of the Municipal Board, Miroslav Stanic. And if I can direct your attention to a couple of portions of that transcript, as you'll go down the transcript, you'll see the name of Pero Jankovic mentioned, and then shortly thereafter you'll see that Dr. Karadzic mentions your name, saying: "Call Radomir Neskovic, vice-president of the Executive Board. I can't deal with that. Nobody has the right to meddle there and, you are" -- it says "the follow", but it looks like "to follow the party policy. You must. You should have come to the party earlier to communicate." Again, a few lines down, Mr. Karadzic says, "You have Radomir Neskovic. Let him deal with it. What kind of influence are they? What are they doing? What do they want?" Ask then further down the page, after a number of brief exchanges, Dr. Karadzic says, "Tell them that I will dismiss the board and appoint other people. You tell them that. I will. It wouldn't be the first or the last time. I will dismiss the idiots who are idiots and who are not implementing the SDS policy. Let them for SPO -- I don't mind, but they won't do that in my party." Now, Mr. Neskovic, do you recall dealing with the president of the Municipal Board, Mr. Stanic? And if so, can you tell us what municipality that is and whether this conversation is a further reflection of the type of interaction or type of efforts that you made that were reflected in the September 10th conversation in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this concerns Stanic, as far as I can remember. The municipality concerned was Vlasenica. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but I think that it concerns Vlasenica. As far as I know, I never went to Vlasenica, to Milici or to Kladanj to try and resolve difficulties of any kind. It's quite obvious that Karadzic is mentioning me here and says that if they have any problems, they should contact me and that I would deal with them. But in practice, they never -- in fact, they never contacted me, and I never went to do anything in Vlasenica, Milici, or Kladanj. I didn't try to resolve any difficulties there because our president of the Executive Board was there, Mr. Rajko Dukic. He lived in Milici, and that was an area where it was easier for him to act. As far as this conversation is concerned, I can tell you they didn't go there and they didn't assign me any task in that respect. Quite obviously, after this conversation they resolved this problem in some other way, without my assistance. So, in fact, I was not involved in this matter. They mention Rajko here. That's Rajko Dukic. Someone called Jankovic is also mentioned; I think he was in Vlasenica or Kalesija. I believe that Pero Jankovic is from Kalesija, and I did not go there. They solved this problem in some other way without involving me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me ask you just about a -- a couple -- and very quickly, I hope -- about a couple of other forms of communication and passing information, orders, guidelines from the top leadership to the other levels. And in that connection, could I ask you to turn to tab 10, please. And if --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, could that be marked next -- it may be already marked, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, tab 10, which contains P64, P65, Treanor 4, tab 57 reflects the minutes of the 6th Session of the SDS Executive Board. And if I could just turn your attention to the second-to-last item, just before the conclusion of the minutes. And that's the second-to-last item in agenda item or number 6, just before the listing of the members of the committee for the annual registration of assets. That says, "It has been concluded that all the members of the Main and Executive Committee of SDS BH are to be involved in the Municipal Committee's work in which area they live." Was that another method of ensuring that the policies of the SDS were communicated to and followed by the lower levels of the party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, this was one of the ways. If I have understood this correctly, this meant that a member of the Main Board who was from a certain municipal territory originally, well, it was his duty to attend sessions of the Municipal Board. I am not sure if I have understood your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question correctly, but that means that all members of the Main Board would regularly attend sessions of Municipal Boards in the territory from which they originally came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally let me reverse that slightly and ask you whether or not the heads of Municipal Boards or other officials from municipalities would themselves visit the leadership figures from the SDS. That is, would they come from the field, from the municipalities, and turn to Dr. Karadzic or other SDS leaders to discuss and resolve certain issues?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Leaders from the municipality, members of Executive Boards or Municipal Boards of the SDS would very frequently go to see Mr. Karadzic. They'd go to the party headquarters for various questions -- for various issues. They'd even go there when it wasn't necessary. They went there very frequently. They wrote letters, they phoned, and there was a lot of contact from the field. They would often visit the party, and when they did, they asked to see Karadzic; they wanted to speak to him about certain municipal matters. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn next to your municipality, Novo Sarajevo, and ask you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask also one additional question in relation to this document. It seems, Mr. Neskovic, under count 6 of the minutes, that you asked for credit for building a house due to your working engagement in the SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that common to seek the assistance of the parties if you were active for the party to get at least support in financial matters, as well? Because I do see that you asked the party, where usually you'd go to a financial institution rather than to a political party. Was that common, such ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, in a certain way. Before I made my request, two other housing matters had been dealt with in this manner for two functionaries. One person obtained money for part of his flat; the other person obtained a flat. And since the party had money, I asked for a loan because there was no other bank; there was no other possibility for me to obtain such a loan. So in a certain way, I was humiliated because although I knew that the party had a lot of money, Karadzic and Dukic told me that they did not have any money and that I could not be given such a loan. So, in fact, I didn't receive anything. My request was rejected, and I did not receive the loan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But these kind of, I would call it a favourable approach to the personal needs of active party officials, was not uncommon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. I made this request in a very open manner, in a legal manner, but there were scores of individuals who managed to solve their personal problems, as far as business is concerned, as far as housing is concerned. They managed to solve their problems in one way or another through the SDS. It's enough to take a list of the people who have flats in Belgrade or a list of people who built houses; whereas, they had no such houses before the war and now they have all of these things, and all of this involved the party in some way. So many people managed to solve their own personal problems; this can be proven today, and they even managed to become rich by virtue of being engaged in the party. And I thought that I could make an open request for a loan that I would pay back, and my request was rejected. I don't know if they rejected other people's requests, but I didn't receive the loan, unfortunately. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to that matter, on page 67 of your interview you said, "[In English] Some people acquired enormous amounts of wealth from these politics, and they were holding high positions. They were given apartments in Belgrade and all over." [Interpretation] Could you clarify what "some people acquired" means exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought that people used the party. There were many people who had no particular importance in the party, but they were on friendly terms with Krajisnik or Karadzic or with some other officials. And then, on the basis of their personal acquaintances, they managed to establish a business, to build houses, to buy flats, and so on and so forth. So this business was not conducted in a transparent manner; it wasn't public. There was an incident that concerned oil of some kind. They said that the SDS had received a lot of oil and that they had received financial assistance from various sponsors, but the party's legal account did not have such money, not even for per diems. On the basis of the experience I had, I never received per diems when I went to certain meetings, when I travelled to certain meetings. I didn't even receive money for accommodation, so I had to sleep over with colleagues. I have nothing that can support this, but there was a rumour according to which very big businesses had been -- were under the auspices of the party, and this was done in a secretive manner. One could now prove that people who are very rich in Belgrade today -- well, one could compare the property they had in 1990 and now. One could compare the property that they were the owners of at the time and now to see what is now the situation. So this business was conducted in an unofficial manner, but I openly asked for a loan. I did not receive the loan, and I am glad they did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you say those who were the friends of Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic, they could establish businesses, buy flats and houses, and so on and so forth, and then you say this was not done in a transparent manner; it was not done publicly. Does this mean that the party and those in leadership positions had money that was available to them? Was the party that rich? Did they have so much money that they were able to give it to -- or to distribute it to people who were friends of the leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The party was poor. The party itself was poor; it did not have such money. I must provide you with another piece of information that concerns the public company which was a company that was jointly owned -- 40 per cent of it was owned by the party, and 60 per cent of it was owned by four individuals, I think. One of the individuals was Karadzic's wife, then there was Miroslav Dokoj [phoen], Dusko Kosic [phoen], and the late Dejan Salinovic [phoen]. So they owned 60 per cent of the shares, and the party owned 40 per cent, and at the assistance of the president of the Executive Committee, Rajko Dukic, who wanted the financial situation to be resolved -- well, although he insisted on this, this was never done. To this very day, we have no idea what that company did, the company called Public [as interpreted]. We don't know what kind of business they were involved in, how much profit they made. We don't know how much money was paid to the party. This was all done secretively, and you couldn't obtain any information in particular because the party was a minority shareholder. And since Karadzic's wife was involved and the other three individuals, they quite simply did not allow anyone to inform the public of how the company was conducting its business. So to this very day, one does not know how business was conducted there; we don't know what the amount of financial transactions was. And as -- that's all I could say about that company. But then it was also possible for a functionary to get a job for some businessman. There was political influence that was exercised, and then you would have such deals. But when you are in power in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are countless possibilities for you to work in a manner that is not transparent. There are countless possibilities for you to become rich in a simple and rapid way. But to this very day I don't know how they conducted their business. I don't know what sort of transactions they were involved in. I can provide you with another example. Luka Karadzic, Radovan Karadzic's brother --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but that was not the purpose of my question. You said that friends of Mr. Karadzic or friends of Mr. Krajisnik were able to become rich by being involved in politics, in inverted commas. Does that mean that they used Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik in order to conduct business, make money, become rich?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether one party used the other party or whether the reverse was the case; I couldn't provide you with any information about that. But there was such business that was conducted in a secretive manner. But as to who used whom, whether one person used someone else or whether there was a deal that involved both parties, well, I really don't know, and I would not like to make any guesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me follow up on His Honour's questions a bit, if I may. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what Novi Privrednik was and its relationship to the party.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about that, and I'm going to tell you honestly what I do know. Novi Privrednik was a company, and I believe Rajko Dukic, Mr. Mirko Krajisnik, Momcilo Krajisnik's brother -- and to what extent Momcilo Krajisnik was involved, I don't know, but these two people were involved. And I think the headquarters was at the Holiday Inn Hotel. And I believe it was a company which did not really have any, I don't know, initial capital or -- or offices or whatever. Maybe it was just a company that existed on paper. I think it was at some point in 1991, and the relations between Serbia and Croatia were extremely tense; maybe there was already a war there. And there were no commercial contacts between Croatia and Serbia. And in my view, this was a company which acted as a liaison between Serbia and Croatia through Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I saw it as an attempt to set up a monopoly with regard to any imports from Serbia. I'm not familiar with any other facts, in terms of their profits, tax situation, gains, or what have you, or -- or who had shares in that company. At any rate, the company was active, and I think Mirko Krajisnik and Rajko Dukic were the main protagonists there. And to what extent Momcilo Krajisnik was familiar with that, I don't know, but he was fairly close to the company, and the headquarters were somewhere in the Holiday Inn. And as to the party itself, the Main Board or the Executive Committee, I don't think it had any influence over the company, and I don't think that there was any sort of cooperation or relationship between the two. In a way, this company was something which is totally apart, which was completely independent, and the party did not really have a formal relationship with it. But they were traders, basically. They did not manufacture anything; they just traded goods at a moment in time when there was a crisis in trade relations between Croatia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that trade in goods included oil and specifically include the company Jugopetrol?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know what they traded in, but, presumably, not trinkets or anything like that. Supposedly, yes, it could have been oil, but I don't know. I never had any insight into what exactly they were trading in. But I think it was on a large scale. They were not a cottage industry or anything like that. There were -- they were doing big business, big deals, and I can't rule out the possibility of oil, in fact, and all the other types of similar commodities that would generally require high excise duties. I can't rule that out, considering who was at the helm of that company and what their positions were, but I have no proof to corroborate that because I've never had an insight into what exactly they did, what their profit margins were, et cetera, and I don't really know who was in charge of the company, who carried out some kind of financial supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I ask you to turn to tab 36 for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 36 is previous Exhibit P64A. It is the minutes of the 8th Session of the Executive Committee of the SDS, held on 6 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, if I could direct your attention to item 3 and specifically item 3(c), which states: "The import of food from Serbia can go on only via Privrednik, which takes a percentage for this." Is -- is that the company you were referring to, and is that a reflection of the trafficking in goods and the -- of --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. Take your time. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the company. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what that percentage was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I think the reference here is to -- I mean, the term "percentage" should be clarified here. I don't know what was the percentage they charged, and I don't know what the quantities involved are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Unless the Judges have additional questions on that subject, I wanted to move on to some of the interactions between members of the leadership and the Novo Sarajevo municipality. And in that connection, could I turn your attention next to tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if that could be marked next in order, please. Oh, I'm sorry, another -- that is already in evidence as P292, but it says "part." Obviously -- I'll obviously be tendering the entire conversation, so I don't know if "part" means that only a portion of that conversation was tendered previously. So I'm a bit in the Court's hands with respect to that logistical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we provisionally assign a new number, and if it turns out that the whole of it was already in evidence but only a part --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- being played, then we could address that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar tells me that P292 is a binder, so "part" could well refer to this intercepted telephone conversation, only part of the whole of that exhibit. So therefore perhaps it's better not to start to assign a provisional number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And between Madam Registrar and myself, I think we can keep an eye on this and resolve the question in the way she suggests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, tab 16, as you can see, reflects a conversation of the 19th of November, 1991, between Radovan Karadzic and Zarko Djurovic. Excuse me. First of all, could you tell the Court who Mr. Djurovic was.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Zarko Djurovic is the president of the Executive Committee of the Municipality of Novo Sarajevo, so that is to say the president of the municipal government in Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware in November of 1991 that Mr. Djurovic and Dr. Karadzic were in contact? Not necessarily the specific conversation, Mr. Neskovic, but just as a general matter.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not aware of this conversation, but yes, they were in contact. I remember -- I can't remember when exactly we had a major problem in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo between the party and the government of Mr. Djurovic, and it was a problem of such a scope that Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic had to intervene. And then Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic together attended such a meeting of the Municipal Board in person in order to use their personal authority to solve the problem because there was a clear conflict between Djurovic, as the president of the municipal authority, and, I think, the president of the Serb Democratic Party in Novo Sarajevo -- I can't remember whether it was Mr. Prijic or somebody else. I'm not sure. But the problem was extremely difficult, and it required the presence of both Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at that very meeting they attended in person. So Mr. Djurovic knew both Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic and -- apart from anything else, had they not known them, they would have been nervous for him to become a candidate and be elected as the president of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one or two quick questions about this conversation, then. On the second page of the English, which I think is also on the second page of the Serbian version in front of you, Dr. Karadzic says, "We'll teach them the law pretty soon because in Novo Sarajevo they block the work of the Assembly." And then he continues about four lines down: "And that we'll probably carry out some kind of reorganisation of the city as such." Mr. Djurovic says, "Exactly." Dr. Karadzic says, "And they can go to fucking hell." Mr. Djurovic says, "Well, so they should." And then there's a discussion about exactly where in Novo Sarajevo are their settlements, and Mr. Djurovic says, "Well, mostly it's Velesici that can be joined to the centre without problems." First of all, when Dr. Karadzic is talking about "their settlement," whose settlements, if you know, would he have been referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can gather on the basis of this, what he means are Bosniak settlements that were built without planning permission. In other words, Bosniaks settled in certain empty areas, and they never got the necessary municipal authorisation, the planning permission. And that happened in a number of places, at Sanac and near Popalici and Velesici, and then problems would arise between the municipal structures, the land register and so on, and they would need to legalise the situation, and so that was the problem. And the municipal authorities were claiming that those Bosniaks were causing problems because they were building houses without planning permission. On the other hand, Bosniaks claimed that they paid good money for certain authorisations, that they basically gave money either to land owners or positions of -- people who had the positions of power. And I think Haris Silajdzic actually intervened, as well, who was the high- ranking municipal official in Sarajevo, and he said, Gentlemen, you pay that money you took from Bosniaks and you give -- you give it back, and then the houses can be pulled down. So that was the problem, the problem with the land register. And, of course, under such circumstances it took on inter-ethnic or nationalist connotations. And I do suppose that Djuric was reporting to Radovan about the situation, and then he replied in his own special way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the next page, at approximately the middle of the English - and as near as I can tell, at the same general portion of the Serbian version - Dr. Karadzic says, "Yes, at the next Assembly session, we must now pass a decision that nothing can be constructed anymore on our territory without the consent of the Assembly and/or some other organ." And then further on down the page after a discussion of the number of people and the number of buildings, Dr. Karadzic says, "Yes, yes. No, that won't do. We'll have to separate all those plots so that everybody -- everybody can be on their own land; right?" And then he asks whose land was it before. Mr. Djurovic tells him that "A lot of the land -- in fact, almost all the land is in our hands." And then he relates that some people may have sold that "before we gained power," which causes Dr. Karadzic to express his dissatisfaction. When Dr. Karadzic is talking about "our territory and everyone on their land," is he there discussing his concern about Muslim settlements on what he considers to be Serbian land?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It is a bit incomprehensible to me; Mr. Karadzic's manner of speaking runs counter to the property laws. There was a great deal of land near Sarajevo and in Sarajevo itself that was legally privately owned by Serbs, and it is widely known that Serbs would sell small plots of land to Bosniaks who used to come from Serbia and Sandzak, and they would sell those plots of land at a very high price, so they got rich; they made good money. And then Bosniaks would build houses on those plots and would settle in those areas. Now, what Mr. Karadzic is saying here does not make sense. I mean, he's talking about the land, but it is not the land owned by either the Serb nation or the party. It is private property owned by private individuals which can -- and which can be disposed of according to their owners' wishes. And I suppose what he meant to say was, If we have too many Sandzak Muslims coming here, the ethnic make-up of the population would shift, or whatever. But Bosniaks replied, We did not snatch it away; we paid good money for this. So we were talking about private business deals between Serbs and Bosniaks, and so one side got the houses and the other side got the money. And it was a huge operation, if I can call it like that. Entire settlements came into being in this way. There were these private deals being arrived at between Serbs and Bosniaks. They sold those plots of land for a great deal of money, and then, for example, Bosniaks would build 50 or 100 houses in a given area, and they would be a big group, and the municipal authorities did not really dare pull those properties down. And so when Karadzic tried to do something about this through Djurovic to try and stop those sales for whatever reason, this does not make sense because this is private property we are talking about. Those were private transactions between individuals, and the land did not belong to other the Serb Democratic Party or to the Serb nation in abstract, but it was owned by private individuals. So I think that this has something to do with the previous topic. Perhaps Karadzic through Dragan Stojic, who was the head of the land register, tried to obtain something in terms of this person using his official position to pull those houses down because adequate planning permission had not been sought and obtained. But I think it is a rather irresponsible kind of interference of politics in people's private lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm about to move on to another subject, which I wouldn't want to truncate, so this would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then we'll have a break and resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to deliver a decision on the oral application made this morning, that is, the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's application made in court this morning for protective measures, that is, pseudonym, image and face distortion, and partial private session for Witness 682. In its oral submissions, the Prosecution recalled the three-part test set out by this Chamber in its previous protective measures decisions. And I specifically refer to transcript page 15.712. It was the Prosecution's submission that all the three factors have been established in the case of Witness 682 and argued in particular that the witness's testimony is likely to implicate persons in killings and other series crimes. The Defence has not opposed protective measures for Witness 682. In this regard, the Chamber would like to express its appreciation to the parties, in particular the Defence in this case, for reaching a common understanding before turning to the Trial Chamber for a decision. The Chamber considers that the requirements for the requested protective measures in this case have been met for the reasons given by the Prosecution. The Chamber orders that Witness 682 testify under pseudonym, with image and voice distortion, and in private session for those portions of his testimony likely to reveal his identity. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm just copying down something from the LiveNote. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, can we next turn our attention to a document found at tab 11 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is in evidence already, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, tab 11 contains the instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions, bearing the date 19 December 1991 and bearing the heading "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, strictly confidential," et cetera. Mr. Neskovic, are you familiar with this document? And if so, can you tell the Chamber whether it was provided to members of the SDS. And again, if so, where and when.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with this document. The Main Board -- or rather, the Crisis Staff did not pass this because SDS did not have a Crisis Staff at the party level. This did not exist, or at the very least, I'm not aware of it, and I should know. I think that, yeah, this is the 19th of December, at the Holiday Inn, at the big meeting room there, so I think that it wasn't a meeting of a body but a kind of -- almost a parliamentary meeting, which would be a meeting to which all members of the Main Board, the Executive Committee, all MPs and all municipal officials, members of the government, the political committee, secretaries and everybody would be invited to. It's a huge meeting. In the Serb culture, you would tend to convene such a meeting on solemn occasions. Anyway, that was the make-up of the meeting. So there was the Main Board with 45 members. It wasn't a separate meeting for the Main Board, nor did the Main Board have a Crisis Staff, nor did it prepare or draw up this document through its own committees. As far as I can remember, this document is something that Karadzic brought into the meeting room, and it had already been completed, printed out. It was in a package, as it were, and in this present form, and he simply put it on the table where the working Presidency was. And I was sitting in the fifth or sixth row, and I left the room on quite a few occasions, so I did not listen to everything, but what I do remember is this: Karadzic had a ready-made list of names, officials out in the field who should be given a copy of that document. I think it was the presidents of the Municipalities, where there were SDS members, or presidents of Executive Committees, if their man was not the president of the Municipality. And as to whether the other members of the Serb Democratic Party were included, I don't remember. Anyway, he would call the names, and as their names were called, they would come up to the Presidency table and they would take a copy of this document, and he said that they were to read it. It was a long time ago, and I'm not 100 per cent sure, but in my view and according to my recollection, he asked for that document to be given back to him, as far as I can remember, in the sense that once they'd read it, they could make a list of the most salient points and then for the document to be returned to him, since it was marked "highly confidential" and it was numbered, as well. So they knew exactly how many copies there were, and the copies were based on the list of names of the people who were supposed to be given the copies of the document. As to whether everybody who received a copy did, indeed, hand it back, I really don't know. And afterwards, this was the famous document that we -- that we used to call the A/B document. Those of us who did not get a copy, who were not on the list -- those of us who were not given a copy, that is, we did not know about the details in the document, but on the basis of our conversations with the people who did get Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a copy, we knew what the gist of it was all about; that is to say, A -- Variant A was where we had majority in the municipalities, and option B was where we were in the minority in municipalities. And as to the Crisis Staff within the Main Board, it did not exist, or else perhaps there could have been a body outside the SDS bodies, the Executive Committee, or the Main Board, and perhaps they would call themselves a Crisis Staff. But as to the actual structure, the official structure of the Serb Democratic Party, there had never been a Crisis Staff at the level of the party itself, as a body that is supposed to lead the party under any exceptional circumstances. And as to what the Main Board did, I mean, they did not draw up this document in the course of their regular proceedings because if they had done so, that would have entailed discussions, a draft text, amendments, and so on and so forth, and basically the Main Board could not have passed a document like this because the party, as any other political party, can't issue orders to municipal authorities. Had the Main Board passed the document of this sort, it would have certainly been addressed to the MPs, and it would have been for them to look into it and pass it. And this was actually in contradiction with both domestic and international law because no political party - and this applies to the Serb Democratic Party, as well - is entitled to issue direct orders to any local authorities or the authorities at any other level, for that matter. So furthermore, this was not the only thing discussed at that meeting. There were other topics being discussed. There were quite a few people there. So it was an emotionally charged atmosphere, and quite simply this parliamentary kind of meeting was not a body that could have changed anything there. It was about getting approval from a kind of Serb -- unofficial Serb parliament for documents that had been drawn up and approved elsewhere. I really don't remember anyone having suggested any amendments or any changes, also because this was a strictly confidential document, numbered, and so on and so forth, and the fact that people's names were called out. And as to whether they did return those copies or not, as far as I can remember, they were supposed to hand the copies back in once they had read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, first, Mr. Neskovic, a very minor question, and that is, Do you recall where the meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: At the Holiday Inn Hotel on the first floor. There's a big meeting room there that can accommodate a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the documents were placed on the table where the working Presidency was. Can you tell the Chamber what you meant by "working Presidency," and who comprised that working Presidency at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure. I think it was Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Miodrag Simovic. But I'm not entirely sure; I can't tell you exactly, but I think that it was Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Miodrag Simovic. And by the way, as to the work of those bodies and structures, a working Presidency would not have any real significance. It would mean that the important people would be sitting at the Presidency table and for them to show their faces to the audience. So it would indicate that those people sitting at the Presidency table would be -- at the top table, would be important people. But basically they did not do anything in particular. They would just been sitting at the top table in order to indicate that they were important, but otherwise they would not play a major role. The president would chair the meeting, Karadzic in this case, and he would suggest the agenda and give the floor to people and take it away from them. And there was some criticism, as well, between Sarajevo, Krajina, and Banja Luka and so on. I think at the time there was some kind of tension there. But anyway, there was this meeting which took place, and this un -- unofficial parliamentary meeting. So everybody would be invited along, and all the bodies and institutions and individuals people who were completely outside these structures, and so you wouldn't know who was there. And then you said, Well, what body made those decisions? And they did not have an answer. It would be everybody and nobody. So that was it, roughly speaking. There were some conspicuous individuals there, or -- some people, such as lawyers, poets, and writers and other people, but they did not actually have a real role there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who received the Variant A and B document from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it should have been given to Zarko Djurovic, who was the president of the Executive Committee, because the president of the Municipality of Novo Sarajevo was a Bosniak, so I think that the document was handed in to Zarko Djurovic. I think it was meant for him. I'm not sure whether he actually attended that meeting, whether he received that document on that occasion or later on. I can't tell you with any degree of certainty. But speaking of Novo Sarajevo, this document should have gone to the president of the Executive Committee, Zarko Djurovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And returning for a moment to the question of the working Presidency. You said you thought it was Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Simovic. I wanted to ask you just a quick question about that. You may recall that you were asked some questions about that during your interview in April of 2004. And at that time, you were asked, "Was Momcilo Krajisnik present at the meeting where this document was distributed?" And you said, "Yes, there were two, three hundred people." You were asked whether he was part of the group that was presenting the document. You said you didn't remember that, there was a working Presidency, and Radovan was distributing this. You even think that he was calling people. And then you said, "But since Krajisnik was sitting next to Radovan, he had access to this document."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate what page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 60, Your Honours. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then finally - and this refers to page 61 - you were asked, "So you recall that Krajisnik was sitting next to Radovan at the front of the meeting." And you answered, "In the working Presidency." You later went on to say you couldn't recall who the other members of the Presidency were, and so I wanted to ask you whether that was consistent with your answer today, that is, that you couldn't recall all of the persons in the working Presidency, but that you do recall that Mr. Krajisnik was one of them.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it figures, because after those talks I was interested in it, and so I asked around, as well, and asked other people whether they remembered. And that's how I got the information from them, as well. Some of them were not certain either, but they said that as far as I could remember -- as they could remember, as well, there was Karadzic and Krajisnik and probably Miodrag Simovic, as well, most probably. I know that Biljana, Nikola, and Jovan Cizmovic were sitting in the first floor. So I stick to my original statement. It is logical, but then I tried to check it out with other people, and I asked around because I just wanted to get a complete picture in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So is this correct: You recall that it was Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at the working Presidency, that is, the head table that Biljana -- that is, Biljana Plavsic -- Nikola, Nikola Koljevic, and Jovan Cizmovic were sitting in the first floor, and then you also checked with other people to confirm whether your recollection was accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that question includes, and it's disguising it -- it includes a question which Mr. Tieger has asked at least once, and he's now pressing to get an answer to a question which he's actually asked and had answered, but he's just wrapped it up in a -- in a more expanded question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you've asked a question about the presence of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour , if the Court is satisfied -- I was only trying to make it as clear as possible. If the Court is satisfied that That question has been adequately answered, I won't be insistent upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just reread it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are satisfied with the answer given, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, was the Variant A and B document regarded as a mandatory instruction by the party members who received it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the membership did not actually receive the document. It was intended only for a limited number of people, and it was a numbered document, as I said before. So I think it was mandatory for those to whom it had been given. And as to the broader membership, they did not have any obligation to read the entire document. Those who had read it could come up with a summary or some kind of interpretation and forward that to the membership. This was for the selected few from the field who had high- ranking positions within the local authorities. And as to the other members, no, it wasn't intended for them. It was up to those people to implement the document. It was mandatory for them, even though the document does not go to -- go on to list any sanctions as to what would happen if they failed to do so. But basically it was mandatory for the document -- for the people who received this document. And then, of course, it was up to them to decide how best to do that, depending on their views and abilities and whatever. Some people did not actually implement the whole thing. Some implemented a little bit of it. And there was no uniformity there, so there were a number of different situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned, sir, that there were about -- between 150 and 200 people attending that Assembly, that parliamentary meeting. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be honest, I can tell you roughly speaking. I didn't actually count the number of members. It was a full house; I think 200 people at the very least. I did not actually count the number of people, but considering the size of the room, it's the biggest meeting room at the Holiday Inn, and it was full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did only the presidents of Municipalities receive the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presidents of Municipalities, if the Serbs were the presidents of the Municipalities; but representatives -- and representatives of municipal authorities if Serbs were such representatives. But when Serbs weren't government representatives or municipal representatives, then it's possible that representatives of SDS Municipal Boards received documents, but I'm not sure. I don't know what the situation is. But if a Serb -- if a Serb wasn't a president of a Municipality or of the government, then I don't know who received the document. These were people who performed their duties in the field and who were on the list, and they would then personally approach the table and take the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was personally provided by Mr. Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this document was provided, did Mr. Karadzic explain the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he spoke in general terms. He spoke about the position of the Serbian people, about the position of Bosnia and of Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth. He told a story within the context of that document. But as far as I can remember, he didn't go into the details of the document itself, but he told the usual story about the position of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, about the disintegration of Yugoslavia, about secession, about the threat of Muslims and Croats. So he mentioned well-known positions, positions that Radovan had spoken about on numerous occasions at such meetings, but I don't remember him discussing the document itself because then the document would have been proposed; there would have been a discussion; there would have been comments; and then another version of the document would have been drafted. No, that wasn't done. This document was distributed such as it was adopted, and no significant changes were made, as far as I can remember. Radovan brought it to the meeting with him. I think that he himself brought it to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did this provoke any reactions on the part of those who received the document? Because -- was there any time for everyone to familiarise themselves with the document in question, and those who received it and who read it, were they able to discuss the document in public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, formally speaking, yes, anyone could have stood up and said, I don't accept this document. Formally speaking, yes. But, in fact, no, they received the document, and then they made certain notes and sketches on the document. I think they then returned the document. I don't think anyone dared contest the document or reject the document or put it into question for any other reason. So those who received the document did not really have much time to keep it on them. They had to return the document. So there weren't really any objections as far as the document is concerned. It was accepted in silence, and then everyone implemented the document to a greater or lesser extent or didn't implement the document later on. This depended on how they viewed everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sorry, but you haven't really answered my question. Mr. Karadzic handed out the document. He did not provide any explanations with regard to the document; that's what you said. Did he allow those who had received the document to read it? That is my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then did Mr. Karadzic start a discussion? Did he allow the individuals who had received the document to discuss the document in public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the discussion was more about talking about the document in an affirmative way. That's what Karadzic wanted to do. He wanted to influence the people there to accept it. It wasn't a discussion that concerned those who were for or against it; it wasn't a discussion that invited those present to make any objections. So it was more a matter of Karadzic defending the document, supporting the document. I don't remember anyone criticising the document, putting it into question, et cetera. No such discussion was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the way the document was presented, those present were not really in a position to voice any objections to it, to contest the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, most of them were not in a position to do so. Perhaps formally speaking those who had received the document could have done so. Only some of them received the document, not everyone there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But please answer my question. Those who were there and those who received the document, were they in a position to make any comments, or was the atmosphere such that it was better for them not to make any comments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they did have that possibility; it wasn't forbidden. They could have taken the floor, and they could have made the comments they wanted to make. But given the atmosphere in the Assembly, given the emotions, given the atmosphere, it was perhaps not conducive to such a discussion because one might have appeared to be a traitor if one rejected the document; one would have been a black sheep. The emotions, the atmosphere in the -- in the room were such that one was not really in a position to contest the document; one didn't really want to contest the document. But in legal terms, one could have taken the floor and one could have contested the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, the emotional atmosphere that - those are the terms you used - the emotional atmosphere that prevailed was one of fear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you could put it that way. One could say that there was fear, fear of being outvoted, fear of Bosniak and Croat dominance. Yes, there was such fear, and that was a key element that contributed to the emotional atmosphere there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: Those who were sitting next to Mr. Karadzic, at the presidential table, did they react in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember. I don't think they did, but I'm not sure. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'd like to turn next to the -- at least some aspects of the implementation of Variant A and B, and in that connection can I ask you to turn to tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And may that -- and that, Your Honour, is a previous exhibit, P529, Hanson tab 378.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, the document at tab 12 reflects a meeting of the Crisis Staff held in the premises of the Novo Sarajevo SDS to discuss the materials received from the SDS BH Main Board. And at the bottom of the page, we see that that meeting was held on December 23rd, 1991. Now, let me give you a moment to look at that document, and I see you're still looking to the binder. Both the English and the -- and the B/C/S should be one-page documents. Now, at the top of the page, after the initial sentence that I related, it says, "First agree," and then it lists a number of items, 1 through 11, although not all included. And we can go over those individually in a moment, but let me ask you first if this was a meeting held to discuss the -- to discuss the Variant A and B document, those -- if that document was the materials received from the SDS BH Main Board.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think so, given the date. This took place on the 23rd of December, and this material was on the 19th, so yes, I think that that is the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let's look quickly at the items listed and the persons assigned. The first item is -- was assigned to Dobro Gajevic and Ranko Jugovic and in the Variant A and B document, under "first agree," number 1 is "Introduce round the clock duty service in all SDS Municipal Boards and ensure constant communication and cooperation with local boards in the territory of the municipality." And was that the assignment given to Mr. Gajevic and Mr. Jugovic because of their positions in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Number 2 is "Ensure conditions for daily meetings of the SDS Municipal Board secretariat." And item 2 in the document -- in the December 23rd meeting in Novo Sarajevo refers to "the appointment of a ten- member Municipal Board secretariat." So that -- that appointment reflected the implementation of item 2 of the first level of the Variant A and B document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just help me. Items 1 and 2, do they refer to Variant B?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you can -- you're more than welcome to look at -- either at the first level of either A and B if you need to refresh your recollection about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would it not be a good idea to first find out whether we are in Variant A or a Variant B situation? I noticed in this respect -- no, let me not say anything. Were you in a Variant A or a Variant B municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was a Variant B one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is that you did not constitute a majority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Tieger, 10 or 11 issues in the first level is something that then becomes a puzzle. Variant B contains 10, as far as I remember, and Variant A contains 11, I would say, instructions in the first level. To the extent you could clarify that during the further examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Neskovic, can you give the Court some understanding of the demographics of Novo Sarajevo at that time in percentages, to the best of your recollection, what percentage was -- of the population was Serb, what percentage was Muslim, what percentage was other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I think that the Muslims were in the majority and then the situation was a little more complicated because at the time there were many people who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs in the census. So who were the Yugoslavs? Were they Bosniaks, Croats, or Serbs? One can't know. Perhaps 10 or 15 per cent of them declared themselves to be Yugoslavs. I think that there were about -- I think the Bosniaks and the Muslims were -- represented a slightly larger half and the Serbs a slightly smaller half, as far as I can remember. I can't remember all the information, but that is the census from 1991. Could I add something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please assist me in relation to Variants A and B because in Variant A there are 11 items, and here in this record there are also 11; in Variant B, there are 9 items. I'm not sure whether the Municipal SDS Board in Novo Sarajevo acted on the basis of Variant A or on the basis of Variant B. In my opinion, they should have perhaps acted on Variant B, but perhaps they acted on the basis of Variant A. So could you assist me? Does this document under tab 12 relate to Variant A or to Variant B?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I should make clear that it's -- we're asking you to assist us. But with respect to the document itself, I think you'll find that it contains both first and second level and both Variants A and B. And as you've correctly pointed out and as His Honour has noted, with respect to Variant A, there are 11 items enumerated and with respect to Variant B, 10. And you may have begun to answer the question I'm about to ask, and I think you've certainly touched on it, and that is, Do you recall whether the municipal officials in Novo Sarajevo, despite the 1991 census and despite your view that Novo Sarajevo should have been a Variant B municipality, took the position that Novo Sarajevo was a Variant A municipality, that is, a Serbian majority municipality, either because they asserted that the Yugoslavs were in fact Serbs or because they asserted that there were Muslims in Novo Sarajevo who shouldn't be there or because they challenged the census or for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to answer the first question there before going on to the possible reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I think it's fair to first establish how those in Novo Sarajevo responsible considered the municipality, whether they considered it to be a Variant A or a Variant B - - whether to proceed on the basis of Variant A or Variant B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, given what I have just had a look at, I think that in Novo Sarajevo the Crisis Staff opted for Variant A. According to Variant B, under item 8, reference is made to a commission, a group of which I was a member, together with Jugovic, Prijic, and Zarko Djurovic. And according to Variant B, that commission should be involved in assessing the necessary number of active and reserve forces of the police and of the Territorial Defence, units of the Territorial Defence, units of the civilian protection, and in accordance with such assessments they should bring them up to strength and take all other necessary measures in order to activate them in accordance with the way in which the situation developed. I think that the individuals mentioned here could not have done what is mentioned under item 8. These are military police duties, and I and Zarko Djurovic were never involved in such tasks. If we have a look at Variant A under item 8, which concerns this group of which I was a member, it states the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are -- I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Tieger. I think the witness answered your question but by a reconstruction such that one could wonder whether a question as to the reasons why would make any sense. It's rather vague, reconstructing what was in his field of expertise, what would you expect him to do as far as the difference in task in paragraph 8 is concerned, then I wonder whether it's of any use to stick to the next question. Did I -- I interrupted your answer. Did I understand you well that on the basis of the tasks assigned that you hardly could expect yourself to be assigned for the task in paragraph 8 of Variant B, whereas paragraph 8 of Variant A comes close to your knowledge and experience? I interrupted you also because it's ten minutes to 2.00, and we would have to stop already at quarter past [sic] 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know that I actually got an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- when I said I -- I asked you whether I understood you well that on the basis of the tasks assigned that you could -- you found it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You remember my question, and you agree with that, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then, Mr. Neskovic, I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether the testimony you have already given or the testimony you still are about to give during the days that come, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom. We'll adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of July, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
